caption:
Who was buried in the Oseberg ship?

In 1904–1905 Gabriel Gustafson and Haakon Shetelig dug a 21.58 metre oak longship out of a burial mound at the Oseberg farm near Tønsberg, Norway. It was a real ship: 15 pairs of oar openings, room for 30 rowers, a mast around 9–10 metres, a sail area of about 90 square metres.

Inside were two women, found together in one bed. One was around 80 and badly arthritic; she also had Morgagni's syndrome, which would have given her a masculine appearance and a beard. The other was first put at 25–30, but tooth-root analysis suggests 50–55. Her broken collarbone was once read as proof of human sacrifice — until closer examination showed the bone had been healing for weeks.

Both ate mainly meat, a luxury when most Vikings ate fish. The younger woman used a metal toothpick. Also in the mound: 14 horses, an ox, three dogs, four decorated sleighs, the only complete Viking Age cart ever found, and more than a hundred fragments of silk — the earliest Viking Age silk known from Norwegian soil. Precious metals were gone; the grave had been robbed in antiquity.

Still open: which woman mattered more, and whether either was sacrificed. The high-ranking woman's identity is unknown. She has been proposed as Queen Åsa of the Yngling clan, and also as a shaman. A claim that the younger woman's maternal line came from the Pontic littoral, probably Iran, was not confirmed by three later studies.

A 2012 replica, Saga Oseberg, sailed the open sea at 10 knots in 2014 — proof the ship was a ship, not just a chamber on land.

Images: excavation photographs from 1904; Narve Skarpmoen, 1926; Jac Brun, 1957; Daderot, 2009. All public domain.
